question: What is the primary function of osteoclasts in bone tissue?

options.D: Resorbing old or damaged bone tissue

explanation: Osteoclasts are specialized cells responsible for the breakdown and resorption of bone tissue, working in balance with bone-forming osteoblasts. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T20#GNS222_U1_T20_h1)

question: Why is damage to articular cartilage notoriously slow to heal?

options.A: It lacks a direct blood supply
options.B: It contains an excess of osteoclasts
options.C: It is constantly exposed to heavy friction
options.D: It lacks a collagen structural framework

explanation: Articular cartilage is avascular, meaning it does not have a direct blood supply to deliver nutrients and healing cells, making regeneration very difficult. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T20#GNS222_U1_T20_h1)

question: What are bony outgrowths that form at joint margins in osteoarthritis called?
explanation: Osteophytes, commonly referred to as bone spurs, develop along joint margins as the bone attempts to repair altered mechanical stress. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T20#GNS222_U1_T20_h2)

question: What triggers the chronic low-grade synovial inflammation seen in osteoarthritis?

options.A: Excessive systemic production of parathyroid hormone
options.B: Shedding of cartilage debris into the joint cavity
options.C: Complete lack of mechanical joint loading over time
options.D: Systemic autoimmune attacks against the synovial membrane

explanation: As articular cartilage breaks down, fragments fall into the joint space, irritating the synovial lining and causing secondary inflammation. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T20#GNS222_U1_T20_h2)

question: What is the term for the invasive, thickened vascularized tissue mass that destroys cartilage in rheumatoid arthritis?
explanation: The pannus is the hallmark inflammatory mass in rheumatoid arthritis that aggressively erodes local bone and cartilage. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T20#GNS222_U1_T20_h3)

question: Which characteristic best distinguishes rheumatoid arthritis from osteoarthritis?

options.A: It is a systemic autoimmune condition involving chronic synovial inflammation
options.B: It is primarily caused by mechanical wear and tear on avascular cartilage
options.C: It involves the formation of benign bone spurs along the margins
options.D: It exclusively affects the weight-bearing joints of the lower extremities

explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is driven by systemic immune processes attacking the synovium, whereas osteoarthritis is a localized, wear-and-tear mechanical joint disease. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T20#GNS222_U1_T20_h3)

question: What is the primary underlying defect in osteomalacia?

options.A: Inadequate mineralization of the organic bone matrix
options.B: Excessive systemic production of matrix metalloproteinases
options.C: Autoimmune destruction of the synovial membrane lining
options.D: Accelerated localized bone spur formation at joint margins

explanation: Osteomalacia is characterized by a failure to properly mineralize the newly laid down bone matrix, typically due to vitamin D or calcium deficits. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T20#GNS222_U1_T20_h4)

question: Why does postmenopausal estrogen withdrawal lead directly to increased bone fragility?

options.A: Estrogen deficiency immediately causes severe systemic vitamin D malabsorption
options.B: Estrogen directly thickens the articular cartilage lining to protect the subchondral bone
options.C: Estrogen is required for osteoblasts to synthesize the initial collagen framework
options.D: Estrogen normally restrains osteoclast activity, so its loss accelerates bone resorption

explanation: Estrogen promotes osteoclast apoptosis and inhibits bone breakdown; when levels drop, osteoclasts become overly active, outstripping bone formation. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T20#GNS222_U1_T20_h4)

question: What is the first physiological event that occurs immediately following a bone fracture?

options.B: Replacement of bone matrix by osteoclasts
options.C: Deposition of a hard woven bone callus
options.D: Formation of a localized fracture hematoma

explanation: Blood vessels tear during a fracture, instantly pooling blood to form a hematoma that initiates the healing cascade. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T20#GNS222_U1_T20_h5)

question: During which stage of bone healing do osteoblasts convert the soft tissue bridge into a hard woven bone callus?
explanation: Osteogenic cells differentiate into osteoblasts during the third stage, laying down calcium and creating a hard bony callus. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T20#GNS222_U1_T20_h5)

question: How does inflammatory joint pain typically differ from mechanical joint pain?

options.A: Inflammatory pain is relieved entirely by periods of prolonged rest
options.B: Inflammatory pain worsens with rest and improves with physical activity
options.C: Inflammatory pain is exclusively triggered by heavy weight-bearing
options.D: Inflammatory pain presents without any associated joint stiffness

explanation: Inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis cause stiffness and pain that are worse after inactivity, whereas mechanical wear worsens with use. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T20#GNS222_U1_T20_h6)

question: A patient following a tibial fracture exhibits severe pain out of proportion to the injury, pallor, and paresthesia in the affected foot. Which condition should the clinician immediately suspect?
explanation: These classic neurovascular signs, especially pain out of proportion and paresthesia, point to rising pressure within a closed fascial compartment cutting off tissue perfusion. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T20#GNS222_U1_T20_h6)
